Ishmael
ISH-may-el
n. (proper)
Hebrew Yishma’el, God shall hear, named by the angel before his birth: because the LORD hath heard thy affliction (Genesis 16:11). Abraham’s firstborn by Hagar the Egyptian, circumcised in his father’s house, blessed with twelve princes, and passed over for the covenant.

Biblical Definition

Ishmael is Abraham’s son by the bondwoman, born of a scheme to help God keep His promise. His name is a permanent record of mercy — God shall hear — and the name is honoured twice: once at his conception, when the angel found Hagar by the fountain in the wilderness, and again when Hagar wept over the dying boy in the wilderness of Beersheba and God heard the voice of the lad (Genesis 21:17). Abraham loved him. When God announced Sarah’s son, the old man’s prayer was, O that Ishmael might live before thee! (Genesis 17:18), and God’s answer granted everything except the covenant: as for Ishmael, I have heard thee: Behold, I have blessed him… twelve princes shall he beget, and I will make him a great nation (Genesis 17:20), but my covenant will I establish with Isaac. He was circumcised at thirteen, the first man in history to bear the sign; he lived a hundred and thirty-seven years; and he stood with Isaac at the cave of Machpelah to bury their father (Genesis 25:9). The angel’s prophecy of his temper — a wild man; his hand will be against every man — came true of his descendants. Paul makes him the type of the flesh, born after the flesh, contrasted with the son born by promise.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 has no ISHMAEL entry as a proper noun, but the English word Ishmaelite had already acquired its proverbial sense of an outcast or one whose hand is against every man — taken directly from Genesis 16:12.

expand to see more

ISHMAEL, n. — The son of Abraham by Hagar the Egyptian; the father of the twelve princes of the northern Arabian desert.

The name means God shall hear, and the marginal note of the Authorized Version at Genesis 16:11 gives it so.

He was circumcised at thirteen (Genesis 17:25), and the Arab custom of circumcising at that age has long been traced to him.

Genesis 25:13-16 names his twelve sons, twelve princes according to their nations, exactly as promised at Genesis 17:20.

A later Ishmael, the son of Nethaniah, murdered Gedaliah after the fall of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 41) and is an entirely different man.

Key Scripture

Genesis 16:11 — "And the angel of the LORD said unto her, Behold, thou art with child, and shalt bear a son, and shalt call his name Ishmael; because the LORD hath heard thy affliction."

Genesis 17:18 — "And Abraham said unto God, O that Ishmael might live before thee!"

Genesis 21:17 — "And God heard the voice of the lad; and the angel of God called to Hagar out of heaven, and said unto her, What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is."

Genesis 25:9 — "And his sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron the son of Zohar the Hittite, which is before Mamre;"

Genesis 25:17 — "And these are the years of the life of Ishmael, an hundred and thirty and seven years: and he gave up the ghost and died; and was gathered unto his people."

Modern Corruption

Ishmael is the standing refutation of the belief that God’s temporal kindness tracks His covenant election — and the standing refutation of the counter-error that those outside the covenant are outside God’s care.

expand to see more

Paul settles the doctrinal use of the narrative in Galatians 4 and Romans 9. Ishmael was born after the flesh and Isaac by promise; these are two covenants, and the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with the son of the freewoman. Every part of the older brother’s position was genuinely advantaged: Abraham’s blood, Abraham’s household, Abraham’s circumcision, and Abraham’s explicit prayer offered for him by name. And the inheritance passed the other way, announced before Isaac was conceived. This is unconditional election stated in narrative before it is stated in propositions, and it is the reason no man may reason from his upbringing, his baptism, his family, or his religious advantages to his standing before God.

The opposite error is to read Ishmael as reprobate, which the text never says. God heard the boy’s cry, opened Hagar’s eyes to the well, was with the lad as he grew, gave him twelve princes and a great nation, and answered Abraham’s prayer for him in so many words — as for Ishmael, I have heard thee. Common grace is real, abundant, and undeserved, and it is not saving. The Reformed tradition has always held both, and the pastoral value of holding both is considerable: it prevents a believer from despising the prosperity of the unconverted and from resting in his own.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Yishma’el (H3458), God shall hear, from shama (H8085) to hear and El, God; his mother is Hagar (H1904), and his sons are the twelve princes of Genesis 25.

expand to see more

Hebrew Yishma’el (H3458) — Ishmael; God shall hear (Genesis 16:11).

Hebrew shama (H8085) — to hear, to hearken, to obey; the verb in his name and in Genesis 21:17.

Hebrew pere adam — a wild man, literally a wild ass of a man (Genesis 16:12).

Hebrew nasi (H5387) — a prince, a chief; twelve princes shall he beget (Genesis 17:20).

Greek kata sarka — after the flesh; Paul’s description of his birth in Galatians 4:23, over against di epangelias, by promise.

Usage

"O that Ishmael might live before thee! (Genesis 17:18) — a father’s prayer, answered and yet not granted the covenant."

"God heard the voice of the lad where he is (Genesis 21:17) — the name made good in the wilderness."

"His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him (Genesis 25:9) — the two brothers at Machpelah."
